rule: Linear A signs are read with the sound values of the Linear B signs that look like them.
allows: value(Linear A sign) = value(Linear B homomorph)
where: §3, pp.3-4; Appendix B opening paragraph, p.36
quote: scholars stretching back to Ventris have long assumed that Linear B sound values could be applied to their Linear A counterparts
examples: every reading in the paper; Appendix B says its signs are "transliterated using Linear B homomorph values" (p.36)

rule: Every sign writes an open syllable: a consonant plus a vowel, or a vowel on its own. The script cannot write a bare consonant.
allows: sign = CV or V; never C alone
quote: As each sign in Linear A is an open syllable, it imposes systematic distortions on Semitic phonology.

rule: Two different signs can stand for the same sound.
allows: value(sign A) may equal value(sign B)
quote: it is indeed possible to encounter two signs that represent the same phonetic value

rule: One sign can be syllabic in one place and a whole word (a logogram) in another.
allows: sign = syllable value OR whole-word value
quote: Signs functioning both syllabically and logographically are not uncommon across ancient scripts.
examples: *301 = /na/ in the formula but stands alone for nawā elsewhere (p.5); *307 = dubur (p.19); *312 = KITNU (p.40)

rule: Stops are not told apart as voiced, voiceless or emphatic, so one stop sign covers all the stops made in the same part of the mouth.
allows: stop sign = any stop at that place: P-series = p | b; T-series = t | d | ṭ; K-series = k | g | q
quote: Stops cannot be distinguished as voiced, voiceless, or emphatic
examples: A-KA-NU = ʾagānu, KA writes /ga/ (p.36); A-PA-RA-NE = ʿibrānī, PA writes /ba/ (p.37); O-SU-QA-RE = ʾO-Sukar, QA writes /ka/ (p.17)

rule: All the s-type sounds share one series of signs.
allows: S-series sign = š | s | ṣ | ś
quote: all sibilants merge into a single S-series
examples: SI-RU-TE = šīrūt, SI writes /ši/ (p.11); U-NA-KA-NA-SI = kanasī, SI writes /si/ (p.9); *301-SI = nāśī, SI writes /śī/ (n.10, p.5)

rule: Throat sounds (laryngeals and pharyngeals) are often not written at all, or are written with a plain vowel sign.
allows: vowel sign V = V | ʾV | ʿV | hV | ḥV; a throat consonant may also be left out entirely
quote: laryngeals are not (always) even written, but represented by a “pure vowel” sign
examples: A-KA-NU = ʾagānu (p.36); A-NA-NE = ḥanān (p.36); U-NA = hunna (p.9); O-SU-QA-RE = ʾO-Sukar (p.17)

rule: Length is never written: neither a doubled consonant nor a long vowel is shown by the spelling.
allows: a written sequence may be read with any consonant or vowel length
quote: neither consonantal nor vocalic length is ever indicated orthographically
examples: JA-DI-KI-TU = Diqqitu with /qq/ from one KI (pp.6-7); SI-RU-TE = šīrūt with two long vowels (p.11)

rule: Linear A does not tell /l/ apart from /r/; one series writes both.
quote: the liquid merger of /l/ and /r/—which the Linear A syllabary collapses
examples: RU = lū (p.9); RA-KI-NI-SE = la-kinnisēt (p.9); SI-RU-TE = šīrūt, RU writes /rū/ (p.11)

rule: Linear A writes a vowel on every syllable, and those vowels carry grammar (case endings, stem vowels, mimation).
allows: every sign contributes a vowel; vowel quality is meaningful, vowel length is not written
quote: Linear A is the only pre-Classical Semitic script that renders full vocalization on every syllable.
examples: the -u of *yaqtulu in TA-NA-RA-TE-U-TI-NU (p.12); the -ī possessive in U-NA-KA-NA-SI (p.9)

rule: The T-series also writes the emphatic ṣ, and (doubled) the interdental ṯ, on top of plain t and ṭ.
allows: T-series sign = t | ṭ | ṣ | ṯ (and d by the general stop rule R05)
where: §6.1, p.12 (for ṣ); Appendix B, pp.36-40 (for ṯ)
quote: I propose that Linear A represents emphatic ṣade through its T-series
examples: TA-NA-RA-TE-U-TI-NU = tana-raṣē-ū-tī-nū (p.12); A-RE-TU-MI = *ʾarṣ-ummī (p.12); A-RA-TU = ʾarṣ (p.37); JA-SU-MA-TU = šāmaṭ (p.38)

rule: The D-series writes /d/ in every reading the paper gives.
allows: D-series sign = d (and t, ṭ by the general stop rule R05)
quote: /di/ Root C₁ of √d-q-q
examples: JA-DI-KI-TU (p.6); DU-RA-RE = durar (p.36); DU-PU₂-RE = dubur (p.19); DA-MA-TE = dmt (p.38)

rule: The K-series writes /k/, /g/, /q/ and /ḫ/.
allows: K-series sign = k | g | q | ḫ
quote: Cf. Heb. yā Diqtu “O Dikte!” (vocative; toponym Dikte/√d-q-q)
examples: U-NA-KA-NA-SI = kanasī, /k/ (p.9); A-KA-NU = ʾagānu, /g/ (p.36); JA-DI-KI-TU = Diqqitu, /q/ (p.6); A-KA-WI-JA = ʾa-ḫa-wi-ya, /ḫ/ (n.41, p.21)

rule: The Q-series writes /q/ and also /k/.
quote: At Troullos, this is O-SU-QA-RE, vocalized as O-Sukar, with a prosthetic aleph.
examples: QA-QA-RU = qaqqaru (n.13, p.8); I-NA-JA-PA-QA = pāqaḥ (p.38); O-SU-QA-RE = Sukar, QA writes /ka/ (p.17)

rule: The P-series writes /p/ and /b/. PU₂ in particular writes /bu/.
quote: The nearest analog to DU-PU₂-RE, or DU-BU-RE, as Davis correctly renders it
examples: I-PI-NA-MA = ʾipinama, /p/ (p.10); DU-PU₂-RE = dubur, /b/ (p.19); A-PA-RA-NE = ʿibrānī, /b/ (p.37)

rule: The Z-series writes the voiced interdental ḏ and the voiceless interdental ṯ.
where: Appendix A, p.36; Appendix B, p.40
quote: ZA-TI ḏāti “of”
examples: ZA-TI = ḏāti (p.36); ZU-RI-NI-MA from √ṯ-w-r (p.40); I-ZU-RI-NI-TA from √ṯ-w-r (p.38)

rule: A doubled sign can mark a doubled (geminate) consonant.
allows: X-X may be read as a single consonant of X, doubled
quote: Elsewhere in the corpus, doubled signs may represent geminate consonants: QA-QA-RU is compatible with qaqqaru “ground”
examples: QA-QA-RU = qaqqaru (n.13, p.8); SA-SA as a possible /šš/ (n.13, p.8)

rule: A doubled SA can mark the sound š (shin) rather than a doubled consonant.
quote: Because the S-series must neutralize all three sibilants (š, s, ṣ), the doubling of SA-SA may signal the phoneme /š/ (shin)

rule: A doubled TE or TI writes the interdental ṯ, the same way a doubled SA writes š.
quote: -TE-TE writes interdental /ṯ/ by doubling convention (cf. SA-SA = /š/)

rule: The vowel of a final sign can be "dead", that is, written but not pronounced.
allows: the vowel of a word-final sign may be dropped in the reading
quote: Variant of A-TA-NA (ZA 9) with feminine -at- written -TE (final vowel dead; √y-t-n “to give”)
examples: AB79 and its inherent /u/ (n.23, p.15); A-TA-NA-TE = yatanat (p.38); SI-RU-TE = šīrūt (p.11)

rule: A pharyngeal ḥ can be dropped from the spelling altogether.
allows: ḥ in the Semitic word may have no sign in the Linear A spelling
quote: pāqaḥ “open (eyes)” (Isa 42:7); ḥ drops (√ʾ-n-n + √p-q-ḥ)

rule: A syllable-final /s/ is left unwritten before a stop, following the Linear B rule.
allows: coda s before a stop may have no sign
quote: coda /s/ unwritten, per the Linear B rule that drops syllable-final s before a stop

rule: Linear A cannot write /hu/, so U-NA is used as the nearest spelling of hunna.
quote: As Linear A has no definite article and cannot render /hu/, U-NA is the closest syllabic approximation to the presentative hunna.

rule: A pre-consonantal /r/ is dropped. The paper states this for the Linear B spelling of a name it compares, not for Linear A itself.
allows: r before a consonant may have no sign (stated for Linear B)
quote: Linear B a-te-mi-to (PY Es 650, genitive) drops the pre-consonantal /r/ per orthographic convention.
examples: A-RE-TU-MI = *ʾarṣ-ummī compared with Linear B a-te-mi-to (n.18, p.12)

rule: *301 is a second sign for /na/, beside the ordinary NA (AB06).
quote: *301 is an allograph of NA: a second sign writing /na/, but one that carries symbolic and semantic weight.

rule: *301 standing on its own is a whole word, most likely nawā "dwelling, temple".
quote: *301 stands alone as a logographic abbreviation, plausibly for nawā “dwelling, temple” itself
examples: 238 of its 291 attestations, mostly Hagia Triada roundels (p.5)

rule: AB79, which the paper transliterates TH or *79, is the only sign for the interdental ṯ, and carries no fixed vowel.
quote: A rare and enigmatic sign, AB79 (𐙀) represents the only dedicated symbol for the voiceless interdental fricative /ṯ/ in Linear A.
examples: A-*79-RA = ʾAṯirat (p.36); *79-DU = ṯudu (p.36); MA-*79 = maṯu (p.36); I-*79-DI-SI-KA = I-Ṯadi Siqqa (p.17)

rule: Scribes usually wrote the ṯ sound with the T-series instead of with AB79.
allows: a T-series sign may be preferred over AB79 for ṯ
quote: Given that AB79 appears in only 25 word-forms across Linear A, scribal convention clearly favored its sublimation into the T-series.
examples: A-DI-KI-TE-TE beside A-*79-RA (pp.36, 15); the TE-TE and TI-TI spellings of Appendix B

rule: *314 writes the pharyngeal ḥ.
quote: *314 𐙦, here read as the pharyngeal ḥ absent from Linear B, is attested six times in the Linear A corpus

rule: AB85 writes two vowels at once, a diphthong, which the paper reads AU.
quote: AB85 bucks the syllabogram trend as a VV diphthong, in the same vein as Linear B a₃ /AI/

rule: *307 is a whole word standing for Semitic dubur, "sanctuary".
quote: I resolved that *307, much like *301, functioned logographically, specifically for Semitic dubur
examples: *307 as a header on Hagia Triada tablets, and after TI-NI-TA on HT 27a (p.19)

rule: *319 may write /hū/, the 3ms possessive. The paper puts this forward conditionally.
quote: If *319 = /hū/: naʿmāṯ-hū “his pleasant one” (fem. + 3ms possessive)

rule: *312 is the logogram KITNU, a linen or cloth item.
quote: Cf. *312 = KITNU (logogram)

rule: RU can write the precative particle lū, "may, let".
quote: U-NA-RU-KA-NA-SI (IO Za 16) inserts RU = lū (the precative particle “may, let”

rule: DU can write dū, a possessive element, "the one of".
quote: du acts as a possessive element

rule: The sign the paper writes I at the end of IO Za 2 is the sign CH008, "hand", and is left untranslated.
allows: final I in IO Za 2 = CH008 "hand" (no reading offered)
quote: GORILA transcribes the last legible sign on IO Za 2 as AB28 (I), though the head-shaped form may be a distinct sign

rule: A- at the start of a word. Three jobs: the 1cs verb prefix "I"; a prosthetic vowel that adds nothing; and the Palaikastro replacement for ya-.
allows: A- = 1cs prefix ʾa- | prosthetic ʾa- | ʾa- replacing ya-
quote: The opening A- is a first-person prefix common to all Semitic languages, followed by a tG stem morpheme (-TA-)
examples: A-TA-I-*301-WA-JA (p.4); A-SI-KI-RA = šēkār + prosthetic A- (p.37); A-SA-SA-RA-ME for JA-SA-SA-RA-ME (p.37)

rule: JA- at the start of a word. Three jobs: the vocative particle "O!"; the 3ms verb prefix ya-; and the first root consonant /y/.
allows: JA- = vocative yā | 3ms prefix ya- | root consonant y
quote: Heading this position, JA or ya functions as a vocative particle
examples: JA-DI-KI-TU = yā Diqqitu (p.6); JA-TA-I-*301-U-JA, 3ms prefix (p.39); JA-SA-SA-RA-ME, root C₁ of √y-š-r (p.7)

rule: TA- inside or at the start of a verb. Two jobs: the tG middle-reflexive stem marker, vocalised -ta-; and the 3fs prefix "may she".
allows: TA- = tG stem marker -ta- | 3fs prefix ta-
quote: The TA- morpheme designates this as a 3fs verb, in contrast to the 1cs A-TA-I-*301-WA-JA which initiated the prayer.

rule: TA-NA- at the start of a verb: the 3fs prefix followed by the N-stem (nipʿal) marker, which survives before /r/.
quote: The NA- that follows represents the N-stem (nipʿal) morpheme, preserved before /r/ where later Hebrew assimilates it

rule: I- . Three jobs: an invariant stem vowel inside the opening verb; the preposition "in"; and a prothetic vowel or locative at the start of a word.
allows: I- = stem vowel i | preposition ʾi- "in" | prothetic i- | locative i-
where: §4.1 n.7, p.5; §5.2, p.10; Appendix B, pp.38 (I-DA-MA-TE, I-KU-PA₃-NA-TU-NA-TE)
quote: Prothetic I- before DA-MA-TE (“the tower”; cf. KY Za 2)
examples: A-TA-I-*301-WA-JA, stem vowel (p.5); I-PI-NA-MA = "in the presence of" (p.10); I-DA-MA-TE (p.38)

rule: U-NA- at the start of a word: the presentative particle hunna, "behold!".
quote: U-NA is the closest syllabic approximation to the presentative hunna

rule: WI- at the start of a word: the conjunction wa-, "and", carrying its own vowel.
quote: WI-PI wīpī “and my mouth”

rule: RA- at the start of a word: the preposition la-, "for".
quote: At Syme (SY Zb 7), we find a short inscription that reads RA-KI-NI-SE, or la-kinnisēt: “for the assembly.”

rule: O- at the start of a word: a prosthetic vowel (the paper calls it a prosthetic aleph).
quote: At Troullos, this is O-SU-QA-RE, vocalized as O-Sukar, with a prosthetic aleph.

rule: DU- at the start of a word: the possessive element dū, "the one of".
quote: du acts as a possessive element

rule: -ME and -MA at the end of a word: mimation, the case ending -am (accusative after ME, oblique after MA).
allows: -ME = -am (accusative); -MA = -am (oblique); both also written as plain "+ mimation"
quote: My reading differs, seeing in ME the Semitic phenomenon of accusative mimation -am: yašāram

rule: -JA at the end of a word. Two jobs: the third root consonant /y/; and the gentilic ending that makes a "person of" word.
quote: -JA functions as the gentilic suffix visible on SU-KI-RI-TE-I-JA “the Keretian” (HT Zb 158b, Hagia Triada)

rule: -TI at the end of a word. Two jobs: the 2nd person object pronoun from the old *-t- series; and a 2fs subject marker on an N-stem verb.
quote: the suffix -TI represents the 2nd person object pronoun from the archaic *-t- series

rule: -NU at the end of a word: the energic nun, an emphatic verb ending, with a vowel after it.
quote: The final NU functions, potentially, as an energic -n

rule: -NI at the end of a word: the energic ending in its -ni form.
quote: Cf. Ug. √ntk “pour out” + energic -ni (cf. Amarna -ni, Heb. paragogic nun Job 19:2)

rule: -TE at the end of a word. Three jobs: the third root consonant; the noun ending -ūt; and a feminine -at with its final vowel dead. A locative -te also appears.
quote: As a verbal noun, √š-r-t (“to minister, serve in a sacred capacity”) produces šīrūt, the cultic act itself.
examples: SI-RU-TE = šīrūt (p.11); A-TA-NA-TE = feminine of A-TA-NA (p.38); I-KU-PA₃-NA-TU-NA-TE, locative (p.38)

rule: -NA. Two jobs at the end of a word: the possessive "our"; and a plural ending after a long vowel. Inside a word it is usually a root consonant or the N-stem marker.
allows: -NA = -na "our" | plural -na | root consonant n | N-stem marker
quote: either Sem. -na “our” + enclitic locative -te, or Hurr. =na (pl. article) + =ta/te (directive)
examples: I-KU-PA₃-NA-TU-NA-TE (p.38); I-PI-NA-MI-NA, final -NA as a plural ending (p.38)

rule: -KA at the end of a word: the 2ms pronoun -kā, "you".
quote: -DE-KA = dī-kā “for you” (relative dī + 2ms -kā)

rule: -DE-KA at the end of a word: the relative dī plus the 2ms pronoun -kā, together "for you".
quote: here read as ʾata-iʿnay-dēka, “who answered for you,” a variant of the formula’s usual opening term

rule: -SE at the end of a word. Three jobs the paper gives it: a gentilic; part of the vessel-label ending -SI-JA-SE; and a Proto-Semitic terminative "toward".
quote: rāmāh + gentilic -SE (√r-w-m)
examples: RU-MA-TA-SE (p.39); A-NA-NU-SI-JA-SE and KI-TA-NA-SI-JA-SE (pp.37, 38); DU-RE-ZA-SE (p.38); MA-KA-I-SE (p.39); U-TA-I-SE (p.40)

rule: -A at the end of a word: the directive ending that marks "toward", the Semitic hē locale.
quote: I-DA-A writes the bare toponym Ida, paired with a final directive suffix (the Semitic hē locale, Hebrew -āh), marking destination

rule: -I at the end of a word: the 1cs possessive "my".
quote: When parsed as a vocalized vowel, the -ī suffix denotes the 1cs possessive, consistent with the 1cs A- prefix at Position 1.
examples: U-NA-KA-NA-SI = kanasī "my assembly" (p.9); WI-PI = wīpī "and my mouth" (p.36)

rule: -NI-TA at the end of a word: the feminine ending -nīt, whose masculine counterpart is -NI-MA.
quote: PN paradigm with I-ZU-RI-NI-TA: “She-of-the-Lion” (√ʾ-r-y + -nīt)

rule: -TE-I-JA at the end of a word: a gentilic adjective built on a place name.
quote: Cf. SU-KI-RI-TA + gentilic adjective -TE-I-JA (toponym + gentilic)

rule: U inside a verb: the indicative vowel *-u of the Proto-Semitic *yaqtulu conjugation.
quote: the U vowel occupies precisely the slot where Proto-Semitic places the indicative *-u of the *yaqtulu conjugation

rule: At Palaikastro an initial JA- is dropped from the front of a word.
allows: Palaikastro spelling = standard spelling with initial JA- removed
quote: The initial JA is consistently dropped: SA-SA-RA-ME for JA-SA-SA-RA-ME, -WA-E for -WA-JA, A-DI-KI-TE-TE for JA-DI-KI-TU.

rule: The same weakening of the y sound may also apply at Zakros, so a word written A-TA-NA would be JA-TA-NA in the standard spelling.
allows: Zakros spelling may drop an initial JA- as Palaikastro does
quote: As a dialectal feature, this weakening of yod may extend to the eastern shore of Zakros

rule: A final -WA-JA can appear as -WA-E, which the paper compares to the Phoenician change bayt > bēt.
quote: the sound changes that distinguish Phoenician from Hebrew can be gleaned as early as the Middle Minoan, e.g. WA-JA→WA-E

rule: The paper sometimes divides a run of signs into words differently from the corpus. Cycle 2 found 16 of 167 rows where this happens.
allows: a paper word may be a part of a longer corpus word, or may join two corpus words
quote: recorded as a single orthographic unit across three sites on Crete, with no break between U and NA
examples: A-KA-NU and ZA-TI, written A-KA-NU-ZA-TI in the corpus (p.36); I-NA-TA and I-*79-DI-SI-KA at IO Za 6 (p.16)

rule: Where the paper thinks a published transcription has the wrong word division, it says so and gives its own.
allows: the paper may reject a printed transcription and substitute its own division
quote: Mis-transcribed by Davis: the tablet reads A-DU 𐄁 ZA, with a word divider; RE is absent.
